newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN defers Cambodian membership, Burma still on.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN defers Cambodian membership, Burma still on.

text.p: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) on Thursday decided to postpone Cambodia's membership in the grouping, Malaysia's national news agency Bernama reported.
Bernama said the foreign ministers had agreed to accept Laos and Burma as new ASEAN members on July 24 during the group's week-long annual meetings.
Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi was expected to make an announcement on the matter at a news conference scheduled for 1530 (0730 GMT) on Thursday.
ASEAN was to admit Cambodia along with Burma and Laos at its annual meeting. But Cambodian Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's power grab over the weekend threw that plan into disarray.
At least 58 people have died and up to 200 wounded in clashes between forces loyal to Hun Sen and those of his rival, First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh.
Malaysia is this year's chairman of ASEAN, which also includes Indonesia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
ASEAN heads of state decided at an informal summit in Jakarta last year to admit its final three members as a group, and left it to their foreign ministers to fix the induction date.
The foreign ministers on May 31 decided to admit the three during July's annual meeting.

The decision was heavily criticised by Western governments and human rights groups that want to isolate Burma over its human rights record and its crackdown on a democracy movement led by Aung San Suu Kyi.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington had "given some advice" to ASEAN for its Thursday meeting. He refused to say specifically what that advice was.

"It's very important at a time like this when there's chaos in Cambodia, when they're on the verge of a civil war, when fighting is occurring throughout the country between forces of the two major political parties, for countries that have an interest in Cambodia to speak out about what is acceptable and what is not acceptable," he said.

ASEAN has maintained that members cannot interfere in each other's domestic affairs, especially when governments of current members range from a communist one-party state in Vietnam, an absolute monarchy in Brunei, an authoritarian government in Indonesia and democracies in Thailand and the Philippines.

But the grouping also has a long history of diplomatic involvement in Cambodia. Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas was an architect of the accords that Washington said on Tuesday had been ruptured by Hun Sen.
In the 1980s, ASEAN supported a guerrilla coalition that included Ranariddh's faction and the Khmer Rouge against the Vietnamese-backed government in Phnom Penh led by Hun Sen.
In Phnom Penh, Hun Sen told reporters before the decision was announced that Cambodia's troubles were "our internal business".
"ASEAN countries must let us solve our problems on our own," he said. "Please stay out of our internal business."
